passages.text: Nevertheless, all of you should know that the bishop toils more than all of you, because each of you suffers his own affliction, while he suffers both his own and that of each person. Therefore, Clement, take the lead as a helper to each person as far as you are able, bearing the cares of everyone. Hence, in undertaking the task of having you administer, I know that I have received a favor, not given one. But take courage and endure nobly, knowing that when you reach the harbor of rest, God will repay you with the greatest of good things—an inalienable reward—because you undertook the greater toil for the salvation of all. Thus, if many of the brothers hate you because of righteousness carried to the utmost, their hatred will do you no harm, but the friendship of the righteous God will benefit you greatly. Therefore, strive to shake off praise arising from injustice, but through righteous administration pursue the beneficial praise that comes from Christ.

lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb denotes strenuous or wearisome labor.
The verb places Clement in a leading or presiding position, here expressly joined with service as a helper.
The verb concerns managing or administering the community and its affairs.
The adjective describes a reward that cannot be taken away.
The expression depicts righteousness extending to its furthest point.
The verb literally evokes hunting and here conveys actively seeking praise.

source_issues.issue: The nested infinitives permit more than one construal. The translation understands the speaker to have undertaken the task of placing Clement in an administrative role.
The supplied print has a raised apostrophe before σωτηρίας although no elision is apparent. It does not affect the translated sense.

passages.text: After saying these things and more than these, he again looked toward the multitude and said, “And you also, my beloved brothers and fellow servants, yield in every respect to the one presiding over truth, knowing this: whoever grieves this man has not received Christ, whose chair has been entrusted to him; and as one who has not received Christ, he will be reckoned as having rejected the Father. Therefore, he will be cast out of the good kingdom. For this reason, strive to come to every gathering, so that you may not, as deserters, incur a charge of sin because of the commander’s discouragement. Therefore, above all else, all of you should give thought to his interests, knowing that, because of each of you, the evil one wages war against him alone with greater hostility. So strive to continue in affection toward him and goodwill toward one another, and to obey him, so that he too may be relieved and you may be able to be saved.”

lexical_decisions.rationale: The term presents the brothers as sharing the status and allegiance of servants.
The participle denotes occupying the leading seat or presiding position.
The literal chair represents the entrusted teaching and governing office without erasing the source image.
This is a military term for those who abandon their assigned rank or post.
The military title continues the image introduced by the reference to deserters.
In this exhortation, the verb means heedful compliance rather than merely hearing.

source_issues.issue: The supplied print has a raised apostrophe before ὡς with no evident elision or syntactic function. It does not affect the translation.

passages.text: But you should also understand some things on your own, because he cannot speak openly on account of the plots. For example, if he is hostile to someone, do not wait for him to say, “Do not associate with this person.” Instead, prudently follow his intention, becoming enemies of those to whom he is hostile and not associating with those with whom he does not associate, so that each person, seeking to have everyone as friends, may be saved by reconciling him and heeding his discourse. But if anyone remains a friend to those to whom he is hostile and speaks with those with whom he does not associate, he himself is also one of those who want to destroy the church. For although he is joined with you in body, since he is not with you in purpose, he is against you—far worse than the enemies who appear openly, scattering those within under the guise of friendship.

lexical_decisions.rationale: The expression contrasts public or unconcealed speech with what must be inferred because of plots.
Although the verb can refer to engaging or contending with someone, the surrounding references to friendship and conversation support a relational sense.
The noun denotes the leader’s purpose or will, which the audience is expected to discern.
The middle participle conveys pressing a claim or striving for the stated outcome.
Here the noun refers to the leader’s speech or instruction that is to be heeded.
The term denotes inward judgment or intention, contrasted with bodily presence.
The participle marks the friendship as seeming or apparent rather than genuine.

source_issues.issue: The antecedent of αὐτόν is unstated. It most naturally refers to the presiding leader, but it could refer to the alienated person. The precise force of the active διαλλάττων—reconciling him, winning him over, or effecting reconciliation with him—is likewise uncertain.
The antecedent of αὐτοῦ is not explicit. The translation takes it as the presiding leader, in continuity with the surrounding instructions.

passages.text: After saying these things, there in the midst of everyone, he laid his hands on me and urged me to sit in his own chair. When I had sat down, he immediately said this to me: “Before all my brothers who are here with me, I charge you: whenever I depart from this life here—as is owed to me—send James, the Lord’s brother, a concise written account, extending even as far back as your reflections from childhood and telling how, from the beginning until now, you have traveled with me, listening to the words and deeds proclaimed by me from city to city. Then, at the end, do not hesitate also to make known the cause of my death, as I said beforehand. For this will not grieve him greatly, since he knows that I have piously paid what I was in every way bound to suffer. Rather, he will obtain the greatest consolation when he learns that after me the teacher’s chair was entrusted not to an unlearned man ignorant of life-giving words and unacquainted with the church’s rule. For deceptive discourse destroys the souls of the listening crowds.”

lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb means to prevail upon or strongly entreat someone.
The noun denotes thoughts, considerations, or reasonings.
The participle grammatically applies to both the words and the deeds, an unusual coordination retained in English.
The noun can mean cause, occasion, or pretext; the requested account of Peter’s death supports “cause.”
The aorist middle presents the necessary suffering as an obligation that has been rendered or discharged.
The noun denotes an authoritative norm or standard and does not necessarily refer to a later fixed collection of writings.
The adjective characterizes the discourse as misleading or capable of leading its hearers astray.

source_issues.issue: The printed period separates the infinitive from the finite verb that most naturally governs it. The translation treats the words as one construction while retaining this as an editorial punctuation feature of the supplied edition.

After the earlier Ἀξιῶ σε, the second accusative σέ creates an irregular construction and could literally suggest sending Clement himself to James. The following context instead concerns sending a written epitome. The translation follows that contextual sense while disclosing the unresolved syntax.

The negation most naturally excludes the whole subsequently described kind of man from receiving the chair, but its grammatical scope across the coordinated participles is loose. The translation takes the unlearned, ignorant, and unacquainted descriptions together within the negated alternative.

The printed period interrupts the description before the participle οὐκ εἰδών. The translation treats the participle as continuing the description and regards the period as an editorial punctuation feature.

passages.text: Therefore I, my lord James, when he had said these things and I had given my promise, did not hesitate, as I had been commanded, to arrange under headings the greater part of the discourses delivered from city to city, which had already been written to you beforehand and sent by him in books, as a kind of reminder, and in this form to send them to you, giving the work the title “Clement’s Epitome of Peter’s Preachings during His Sojourns.” But I will now begin to set it out as I was commanded.

lexical_decisions.rationale: The participle records Clement’s promise before describing his prompt fulfillment of it.
The expression denotes the bulk or most of the material rather than necessarily all of it.
The noun refers to principal points or summary headings used to organize an epitome.
Literally a sign or marker, it here describes the summary’s function as an aid to recognition or recollection.
The adjective associates the preachings with Peter’s presence or stays in the places he visited.
The verb marks the transition from the prefatory letter to presenting the promised material.

source_issues.issue: The accusative participle is syntactically unusual with the first-person subject of οὐκ ὤκνησα; it may align with an understood accusative subject of the dependent infinitives. The translation renders it as an action performed by Clement without altering the supplied form.

The title can describe preachings delivered during Peter’s stays in various places, preachings associated with his visits, or more generally local or public preachings. The translation chooses the sojourn sense without treating the wording as corrupt.
